posts.name: mohsendev
posts.cooked:
Hi everyone,

I’m using Grok Bot on a Pro+ plan. I noticed that when using custom bots for discussion/consultation sessions (text-only prompt engineering, no codebase editing or agent file creation), the token accumulation scales up extremely fast. A single prompt run can register 249K+ tokens behind the scenes.

I understand that the conversation context builds up with every turn, but for a text-based consultation, this burns through the usage pool very quickly.

Is there a recommended workflow to compact or prune the context window during a long session with a custom bot without losing its core prompt instructions? I’d love to know how other users manage their token consumption during theoretical design meetings with their bots.

image651×220 5.78 KB

image1099×631 56.5 KB

posts.name: Mohit
posts.cooked:
Hey @mohsendev! This is expected: every reply re-reads the bot’s whole conversation, so each usage row is roughly the conversation size (mostly cached tokens), not your message. It only auto-summarizes near the model’s limit, and there’s no manual compact yet (it’s a request we’re tracking).

To reset cost mid-session: ask the bot for a short handoff summary, then right-click it in the sidebar → Duplicate. The copy keeps its name, instructions, routines and avatar but starts with an empty conversation. Paste the summary as its first message and keep core instructions in Edit Profile (not chat) so they always carry over.

More on this here: Grok Bot: prune/compact an agent’s context without creating a new Bot.

posts.name: mohsendev
posts.cooked:
Hi everyone, and special thanks to @mohitjain for the workaround recommendation.
I’ve spent the last few hours running rigorous, isolated benchmark tests on my Pro+ account (starting from a clean 0% weekly reset) to track exactly where our token quotas are disappearing. The results are eye-opening and fully expose the architectural flaws of the current system. Here is the data-driven breakdown of what is actually happening behind the scenes:

1. The Multi-Bot “Fleet Tax” is Exponential (and Destructive)

In group chats (Multi-Bot rooms), even in a brand new, empty room with zero message history, typing a single short prompt like “Where did we leave off?” immediately injected 149.4K tokens on the first turn! Within 5 minutes of sitting idle, background loops/routines between the bots caused a massive, silent text dump, cycling from 130K to 273K tokens repeatedly without a single keystroke from my end. The system forces a massive “context tax” by blindly injecting the identity blueprints and skill catalogs of ALL bots in the room simultaneously, hitting what I am highly confident is a hard 300K limit/cap (though further official verification is needed) almost instantly.

2. Testing the @mohitjain Workaround (Isolated 1:1 Tests)

I isolated my quality bot to a clean 1:1 conversation to test the Duplicate + Handoff Summary workflow:

  • The Original Room Baseline: Stood heavily at 158.8K input tokens due to the bot being continuously hooked to read a large 16,000-line repository.
  • The Duplicate Room (Turn 1): After dumping the comprehensive text summary into the freshly cloned room, it successfully smashed the historical bloat, plunging the baseline down to just 35.7K tokens! A massive 75% token reduction. The workaround absolutely works to clear operational debt.

3. The Catch: The “Lazy Loading” Background Loop

However, the most fascinating discovery came on Turn 2 in the newly duplicated room. The moment I drilled down into specific code implementation details (asking for Jenkinsfile and package.json modifications), a massive background injection loop triggered automatically. Over the span of two minutes, the active input size crawled vertically: 38K → 43K → 49K → 57K → 61K → 67K tokens.
This proves the engine uses a Lazy-Loading Context Injection mechanism. Even if you wipe the chat history clean via duplication, the very instant your prompts look for deep code assistance, the backend starts aggressively pulling and parsing secondary project files under the hood to construct the response, rapidly rebuilding the snowball effect.

Conclusion & Strategic Workflow:

This massive overhead means we are burning through our token quotas at an unsustainable rate for simple text consultations, primarily because the platform severely lacks an on-demand skills architecture or indexed file-filtering.
Until a native Compact / New Session button is officially shipped to prune text history dynamically, the only sustainable way to keep our quotas alive is The 4-Turn Duplication Rule:

  1. Completely abandon multi-bot group chats for long code reasoning.
  2. Conduct deep work in 1:1 rooms, allowing the bot to lazy-load what it needs for 3 to 4 turns.
  3. Once the active token count starts creeping past 120K+, pull a concise 5-line Handoff summary, duplicate the bot, and start fresh.

I hope the dev team looks closely at these logs to optimize how project codebases are injected during deep chat sessions. Looking forward to a permanent fix!

posts.name: Heuristico LAB
posts.cooked:
@mohsendev That breakdown on the lazy-loading background injection loop (climbing from 38k to 67k tokens the moment secondary files are touched) identifies the core structural bottleneck with file-based agent loops.

When the agent attempts to resolve imports or config linkages, background indexing lazily ingests full implementation bodies of peripheral dependencies rather than their interface boundaries. This redundant code inflates the context past 150k+ tokens, degrading model attention via the lost-in-the-middle effect and compounding cache-read costs on every subsequent turn.

Workarounds like manual handoff duplication clear debt temporarily, but the underlying issue is the lack of AST-level boundary enforcement before context injection.

To address this deterministically at the protocol layer, we open-sourced **`ctxfw`** (Context Firewall).

It runs locally as a stdio MCP server using native Tree-Sitter C-bindings to prune source files in-memory before the agent context engine ingests them:
* **Target file ($D_0$):** 100% full implementation retained.
* **Direct dependencies ($D_1$):** Function/class bodies are pruned into typed interface stubs (`...`), preserving docstrings, parameter types, and return contracts.
* **Transitive imports ($D_{2+}$):** Compacted to nominal symbol declarations.

**Empirical benchmarks:**
* **Latency:** <60 ms (54 ms mean) via native Tree-Sitter C-bindings.
* **Token reduction:** 72.4% token mass eliminated on polyglot dependency graphs without semantic loss.
* **Zero egress:** 100% local in-memory execution via stdio; zero network telemetry.
* **Verification:** Grade A certified on the Glama MCP Directory under containerized JSON-RPC audit suites.

#### Cursor Integration

1. Install via pip (`ctxfw` on PyPI):
```bash
pip install --upgrade ctxfw
ctxfw doctor
  1. Add to your .cursor/mcp.json:

JSON

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "ctxfw": {
      "command": "ctxfw-mcp",
      "args": ["--root", "."]
    }
  }
}

When registered, the agent queries ctxfw to resolve interface stubs for peripheral codebase dependencies instead of ingesting raw source bodies, preventing the lazy-load snowball from exhausting context quotas across multi-turn sessions.
